transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Torres (KiwiWare Head of ML), Greg O'Neal (CTO), Priya Sethi (Eng Manager)
Recording link: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/FF-20260407-KW-001 (note: demo deck link shared in chat)

Summary (auto): Quick kickoff for a 3-week POC focusing on integration via Redwood SDK + OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Primary goals: ensure function/tool calling works for downstream orchestration, validate structured JSON output reliability, meet latency and cost targets under replayed production load. Security checklist: SOC2 compliance, VPC/private deployment options, KMS integration for keys.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick roll call and then we'll jump into scope. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Samir our SE.
[00:07] Samir: Hi all. Real quick — I put a short agenda in the chat: success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, then integration approach.
[00:14] Lina: Great, thanks. I'll just say up front our primary driver is interactive latency for our user-facing assistant. So, we need 95th percentile under, uh, roughly 300 milliseconds ideally, and the output needs to be strict JSON since it feeds downstream systems.
[00:28] Greg: And on the infra side, we need to keep keys in our KMS, and we have to stay within a VPC for the pilot. SOC2 is required for procurement but that's later in the checklist.
[00:37] Maya: Perfect. Samir, maybe you can start with how we'd measure latency and the benchmark harness?
[00:41] Samir: Sure. So the plan we suggested — two-phase. Phase 1 is a replay of your production traces to get baseline token distributions and latency under Redwood's hosted and dedicated configs. We'll provide a replay harness (python + simple curl/async script) and an example Jupyter that computes p50/p95/p99. Phase 2 is synthetic stress tests for concurrency and batching behavior.
[01:05] Priya: When you say "hosted and dedicated" what's the tradeoff? We're worried about cost — dedicated reserved capacity sounded expensive.
[01:11] Samir: Right. Hosted gives fastest time-to-value, pay-as-you-go; dedicated reduces per-token cost at scale and gives predictable throughput — plus isolation. For this POC we can run hosted in a private VPC edge region to satisfy network controls, or demo dedicated if you want to evaluate throughput economics.
[01:26] Lina: For benchmarks, our typical traffic is bursts up to 160 req/min during peak, average 60 req/min. Average prompt size ~450 tokens, average completion ~180 tokens. Does that map to your batching model?
[01:38] Samir: Yes — good numbers. We'll configure continuous batching with target latency SLOs — and we'll test with different batch sizes. Important to capture KV cache warmup for multi-turn flows — sometimes the first few requests are slower.
[01:50] Greg: Is the KV cache something we need to manage? Or is that internal?
[01:53] Samir: It's internal to the runtime. We expose configuration knobs — e.g., per-session cache TTL and whether to pin certain keys. Might be misheard in transcripts but it's K V cache.
[02:02] Lina: Ok. On function calling: our orchestrator expects the LLM to emit a JSON object with fields {action, args}, where args may include nested structures. We need the model's structured outputs to be strictly validateable against a JSON schema.
[02:13] Maya: Redwood supports structured output and function/tool calling — our OpenAI-compatible endpoints accept a functions array and will surface the function call in the response for deterministic parsing.
[02:22] Samir: We'll demonstrate both approaches: 1) model-based JSON generation validated with a schema plus a post-parse verifier, and 2) explicit function calling where the model returns a function_name and arguments. For the latter, we can hook into your tool endpoints directly during the POC.
[02:36] Priya: How do you handle hallucinations for structured outputs? If the model invents fields, that breaks downstream.
[02:41] Samir: Good question. We'll evaluate a set of prompts and a small eval suite to measure structural accuracy — F1 on required fields, plus end-to-end validation rate. We also recommend using a light deterministic postprocessor (e.g., schema validator that rejects or repairs responses) and a fallback policy to re-query or use a lower-latency cached answer.
[03:02] Lina: Success criteria: I'll propose p95 latency < 300ms on replayed workload, structural validation pass rate > 95% for required fields, and cost under $0.40 per 1k tokens equivalent for inference during pilot. Thoughts?
[03:15] Maya: Those are reasonable starting targets. We may have to relax or tighten depending on model variant and quantization. We'll include cost estimates for different model families in the pricing sheet.
[03:25] Greg: Security — we need KMS integration and audit logs exported to our SIEM. Can Redwood integrate with GCP KMS or Azure Key Vault?
[03:33] Samir: Yes — we support KMS integrations for key wrapping and also can push audit logs to your Syslog/ELK/ SIEM via our private deployment or via Secure Forwarder for hosted. We'll attach SOC2 package and a short runbook.
[03:47] Priya: About latency, are you testing on GPUs with attention optimizations or CPU quantized runtimes? We have a mix in our infra.
[03:55] Samir: For interactive low-latency we typically recommend GPU-backed inference with AVX/attention kernels; but for cost we can evaluate int8 quantized runtimes. Part of the benchmark will include latency/throughput tradeoffs per variant.
[04:08] Maya: Ok let's walk through the timeline we think is feasible for a 3-week pilot. Week 0 (this week) — alignment & data handoff; Week 1 — replay and baseline results; Week 2 — targeted tuning, function-calling flows; Week 3 — final report, cost/latency tradeoffs, and pilot signoff.
[04:26] Lina: That timeline is tight but doable. We need to get you traces ASAP. Also, who owns the infra during pilot — do we provide a staging cluster?
[04:34] Samir: You can do either. For fastest onboarding we run hosted in a VPC with a short-lived service account, but if you prefer we can run Redwood Private on your staging cluster — that adds setup time. For pilot, hosted-VPC is usually the sweet spot.
[04:48] Greg: For metrics we'll want p50/p95/p99 latency, token counts, cost per 1k tokens, success rate on structured outputs, and error breakdowns.
[04:57] Samir: We can provide dashboards for all those — and we'll instrument token-level breakdowns in Redwood Console.
[05:03] Priya: Any blockers on our side? Data sharing is the main one — we need legal sign-off to share traces.
[05:09] Maya: Understood. We'll treat that as an action item — we can take a sanitized subset and sign the DPA if needed.
[05:15] Lina: Also, can you show a quick demo of function calling now? I know it's a short call but a very small demo would be helpful.
[05:21] Samir: Absolutely, I have a short script. (screen share) Ok, sending a sample request to the OpenAI-compatible endpoint with functions array... and you can see the response returns a function_call object with name and arguments as JSON. Sometimes the transcriber writes this as "function calling" or "function calling object" but the payload is explicit.
[05:45] Greg: Looks good. Does the SDK auto-retry on network failures? We need idempotency controls.
[05:50] Samir: SDK has retry hooks and you can set idempotency keys; we also recommend at-most-once semantics for function executions via your orchestrator.
[05:59] Priya: For structured fields with nested arrays, will the schema validation add noticeable latency?
[06:05] Samir: Minimal — schema validation is done client-side or in a lightweight edge step, not in the core generation path. We can show the end-to-end timing in week 1 benchmarks.
[06:13] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps. Samir will share the benchmark harness and a sample replay script by Friday. Maya will send the pricing and pilot contract. KiwiWare will provide traces and infra access details. We'll schedule the SE install session week of April 20. Anything else?
[06:27] Lina: Please also include an example of function calling with nested args and a sample JSON schema we can test against.
[06:33] Samir: Noted — will include.
[06:36] Greg: Also, can you include a short note on fallback policies — e.g., model fallback to cheaper variant if latency spikes?
[06:42] Maya: Yes, we'll include fallback policy patterns and how routing works (region/model/capacity tiers).
[06:48] Priya: Great. Thanks everyone.
[06:50] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with artifacts.
[06:53] (end)
